G1.abbott_html: alpha, the first letter of the Greek alphabet. As a numeral, αʹ = 1, α͵ = 1000. As a prefix, it appears to have at least two and perhaps three distinct senses: 1. ἀ- (before a vowel, ἀν-) negative, as in ἄ-γνωστος, ἄ-δικος. 2. ἀ-, ἁ- copulative, indicating community and fellowship, as in ἁ-πλοῦς, ἀ-κολουθέω, ἀ-δελφός. 3. An intensive force (LS, s. α), as in ἀ-τενίζω is sometimes assumed (but v. Boisacq, s.v.).

G25.abbott_html: to love, to feel and exhibit esteem and goodwill to a person, to prize and delight in a thing. 1. Of human affection, to men: τ. πλησίον; τ. ἐχθρούς; to Christ; to God; c. acc. rei. 2. Of divine love; (a) God's love: to men; to Christ (b) Christ's love: to men; to God; c. cogn. acc. SYN.. From its supposed etymology ἀ. is commonly understood properly to denote love based on esteem (diligo), as distinct from that expressed by (amo), spontaneous natural affection, emotional and unreasoning. If this distinction holds, ἀ. is fitly used in NT of Christian love to God and man, the spiritual affection which follows the direction of the will, and which, therefore, unlike that feeling which is instinctive and unreasoned, can be commanded as a duty. (Cf. and v. Tr. Syn. §xii; Cremer, 9, 592; and esp. MM, VGT, s.v.)

Of divine love; (a) God's love: to men; to Christ (b) Christ's love to men. 3. In pl. love feasts: (DB, iii, 157). SYN.. ἀ. signifying properly love which chooses its object, is taken over from LXX, where its connotation is more general, into NT, and there used exclusively to express that spiritual bond of love between God and man and between man and man, in Christ, which is characteristic of Christianity. It is thus distinct from, friendship ( only), natural affection (in NT only in compounds, v.s. ) and, sexual love, which is not used in NT, its place being taken by. (Cf. and v. Abbott, Essays, 70f. DB, vol. i. 555; Cremer, 13, 593; MM, VGT, s.v.).
